subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Fungi cause a spectrum of infections from superficial skin disease to life‑threatening systemic mycoses. Understanding host risk, typical presentations, limited diagnostics and pragmatic treatment is essential for clinicians in East African hospitals.

sections.p: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with cell walls containing chitin and β‑D‑glucan. In humans they act as opportunistic pathogens when immunity is impaired or skin barriers are broken.
b: Broad categories: superficial, subcutaneous, opportunistic systemic, endemic dimorphic.
Key hosts: HIV/AIDS, diabetes, malnutrition, steroid use, chemotherapy.

sections.p: Most pathogenic fungi grow as yeasts (single cells) or hyphae (filamentous). Dimorphic species exist as molds in the environment and as yeasts in tissue.
b: Cell wall components (chitin, β‑D‑glucan) trigger immune response.
Thermal dimorphism allows survival at 25 °C (environment) and 37 °C (human).

sections.p: Fungi reach the host by inhalation, direct skin contact, or via contaminated medical devices. Endemic dimorphic fungi are acquired from soil; Candida spreads from endogenous flora.
b: Inhaled conidia → pulmonary infection → hematogenous spread (e.g., Histoplasma).
Skin breach → subcutaneous infection (e.g., Sporotrichosis).

sections.p: Clinical disease depends on organism and host immunity. In low‑resource settings the most common are:
b: Superficial: tinea corporis, onychomycosis – itchy, ring‑shaped lesions.
Mucocutaneous: oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis – painful white plaques, dysphagia.
Opportunistic systemic: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), disseminated candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis – fever, respiratory failure, meningeal signs.
Endemic dimorphic: Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis – chronic cough, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly.

sections.p: Limited laboratory capacity requires a stepwise approach: clinical suspicion, bedside microscopy, and targeted tests when available.

t.a: KOH wet mount of skin scrapings
t.b: Confirms presence of fungal hyphae or yeast; a positive result supports tinea or candidiasis.
Detects encapsulated yeast of Cryptococcus; a positive result confirms cryptococcal meningitis.
Elevated in PCP and many invasive fungi; helps when culture unavailable. If unavailable, rely on clinical picture and radiology.
Shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates in PCP or cavitary lesions in histoplasmosis; guides further testing.

t.a: Culture on Sabouraud agar (if lab present)
t.b: Identifies species; not essential for immediate management in resource‑limited settings.

sections.p: Therapy combines antifungal agents with correction of underlying immunosuppression where possible.
b: Fluconazole – first‑line for most Candida mucocutaneous disease and cryptococcal meningitis (induction 2 weeks, then consolidation). Chosen for oral availability and low toxicity.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate – preferred for severe disseminated candidiasis, PCP, and endemic dimorphic infections when IV access possible; avoided if renal function unknown.
Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole – drug of choice for PCP; also covers some bacterial co‑infections. Avoid in severe sulfa allergy.
Adjunctive measures – control diabetes, reduce steroids, start antiretroviral therapy in HIV, ensure clean wound care.

t.b: Needed when using amphotericin B; if labs unavailable, watch for rising creatinine symptoms (oliguria, fatigue).

t.a: Therapeutic drug monitoring for fluconazole (if available)
t.b: Ensures adequate levels in meningitis; if unavailable, use standard duration and clinical response.

b: Distinguish PCP (dry cough, normal chest X‑ray early, β‑D‑glucan ↑) from bacterial pneumonia.
Remember cryptococcal meningitis presents with raised intracranial pressure; therapeutic lumbar puncture is lifesaving.
In HIV patients with CD4 < 200 cells/µL, any oral thrush warrants evaluation for esophageal candidiasis.
When cultures are not possible, a KOH positive result is sufficient to start topical azoles for tinea.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid respiratory deterioration in suspected PCP or disseminated candidiasis.
Altered mental status with meningeal signs – suspect cryptococcal meningitis.
Severe renal impairment after amphotericin B initiation.

faq.q: Why is β‑D‑glucan not specific for a single fungus?
faq.a: It is a cell‑wall component of many yeasts and molds, so elevation indicates invasive fungal infection but not the exact species.

faq.q: Can topical antifungals treat systemic disease?
faq.a: No; they only act on skin or mucosal surfaces. Systemic disease requires oral or IV agents.

faq.q: What is the first step if a patient cannot afford fluconazole?
faq.a: Use high‑dose itraconazole if available, or consider amphotericin B deoxycholate despite toxicity, after weighing risks.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV patient with CD4 150 presents with dry cough and hypoxia – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order β‑D‑glucan and a chest X‑ray; a positive β‑D‑glucan with interstitial infiltrates points to PCP, prompting TMP‑SMX therapy.

A febrile child with a chronic ulcer on the hand after a thorn injury – which fungus is most likely and how would you confirm it? — Suspect Sporothrix schenckii; perform KOH mount and culture on Sabouraud agar; a cigar‑shaped budding yeast at 37 °C confirms diagnosis.

You have a patient with meningitis signs, elevated opening pressure, and India ink shows encapsulated yeast – what is the immediate management? — Start high‑dose fluconazole (or amphotericin B if severe) and perform therapeutic lumbar puncture to relieve pressure.

A diabetic patient presents with intertriginous erythema and satellite papules – what is the most likely organism and first‑line therapy? — Candida species; treat with topical azole (clotrimazole) and improve glycemic control.

In a resource‑limited hospital, cultures are unavailable; how do you diagnose PCP? — Rely on clinical picture (dry cough, hypoxia), chest X‑ray showing diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and a positive serum β‑D‑glucan; start TMP‑SMX empirically.

Why is amphotericin B avoided in a patient with known chronic kidney disease, and what alternative can be used for severe cryptococcal meningitis? — Amphotericin B is nephrotoxic; fluconazole can be used for induction if renal risk outweighs benefit, monitoring intracranial pressure.

A patient on long‑term steroids develops oral white plaques that can be scraped off – what is the diagnosis and why must you look for esophageal involvement? — Oral thrush (candidiasis); in immunosuppressed hosts it often extends to the esophagus causing dysphagia, requiring systemic therapy.

How does HIV infection predispose to fungal infections and which immune cell is most important? — CD4+ T‑lymphocytes orchestrate cell‑mediated immunity; their depletion impairs clearance of intracellular fungi like Pneumocystis and Cryptococcus.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and systematic physical exam allow rapid discrimination between superficial, subcutaneous, opportunistic and endemic fungal infections, even when laboratory support is minimal.
b: Onset and duration of skin or respiratory symptoms (acute vs chronic).
Exposure history: travel to endemic areas, soil work, animal contact, recent construction, use of corticosteroids or chemotherapy.
HIV status, CD4 count, diabetes control, malnutrition, pregnancy, renal or hepatic disease.
Recent antibiotic or broad‑spectrum antifungal use, indwelling catheters, ventilator support.
Symptoms of systemic spread: fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, dyspnea, headache, visual changes.

t.b: Look for lesion pattern (ring‑shaped, scaly, ulcerated, nodular). Positive ring‑shaped lesion suggests tinea corporis; nodular lymphangitic spread suggests sporotrichosis.
Gentle pressure around erythematous patches. Presence of satellite papules supports candidal intertrigo.
Scrape oral or esophageal plaques with a tongue depressor. White plaques that wipe off leaving erythema indicate Candida; non‑wiping plaques suggest other etiologies.
Diffuse crackles may indicate PCP or endemic dimorphic pneumonia; absent findings do not exclude early disease.
Look for papilledema or cryptococcal choroiditis; absence does not rule out meningitis.
Opening pressure >250 mm H2O suggests cryptococcal meningitis; CSF appearance alone cannot differentiate fungal from bacterial meningitis.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise algorithm: bedside microscopy, rapid antigen or molecular tests, then culture or histopathology when resources allow.
b: Direct KOH mount of skin scrapings or sputum – answers “is there fungal elements?” Positive hyphae or yeast confirm presence; cannot identify species.
India ink of CSF – answers “is Cryptococcus present?” Encapsulated yeast seen = positive; sensitivity ~70 %.
Serum (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan – answers “is there invasive fungal infection?” Value ≥80 pg/mL supports PCP, candidemia, or invasive aspergillosis; false‑positive with hemodialysis filters.
Cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay (CrAg LFA) – answers “is Cryptococcus present?” Positive in serum or CSF confirms diagnosis; titers guide severity.
Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain of tissue – answers “what morphology is present?” Budding yeasts with capsule = Cryptococcus; narrow‑based buds = Blastomyces.
Chest X‑ray – answers “is there pulmonary infiltrate?” Diffuse interstitial pattern suggests PCP; focal cavitary lesion suggests Histoplasma or Blastomyces.
If culture unavailable: rely on clinical algorithm plus rapid tests; treat empirically according to most likely pathogen.

t.b: Detects fungal cell walls; presence of septate hyphae = dermatophyte, pseudohyphae = Candida. Negative does not exclude deep infection.
Elevated ≥80 pg/mL supports invasive fungal disease; normal <60 pg/mL makes fungal infection unlikely.
Positive result = cryptococcal infection; quantitative titer >1:1024 predicts high intracranial pressure.
Diffuse ground‑glass opacity = PCP; miliary nodules = disseminated histoplasmosis; cavitary lesion = blastomycosis.
Elevated protein >100 mg/dL, low glucose <40 mg/dL, lymphocytic predominance suggest fungal meningitis; not specific without antigen.
Visualizes organism morphology; broad, ribbon‑like aseptate hyphae = Mucorales; narrow‑based buds = Blastomyces.

sections.p: Apply disease‑specific criteria to decide on inpatient versus outpatient management and to gauge prognosis.
b: PCP: Diagnosis = compatible clinical picture + positive (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan or PCR; severity = PaO2 <70 mm Hg or A‑a gradient >35 mm Hg.
Cryptococcal meningitis: Diagnosis = positive CSF CrAg or India ink; severity = opening pressure >250 mm H2O or CSF CrAg titer >1:1024.
Disseminated candidiasis: Diagnosis = positive blood culture or sterile‑site tissue with yeast; severity = ≥2 organ systems involved or septic shock.
Endemic dimorphic infection (Histoplasma, Blastomyces): Diagnosis = compatible exposure + antigen detection in urine/serum or tissue; severity = hepatic involvement, hypoxia, or >30 % weight loss.
Superficial tinea: Diagnosis = clinical + KOH; severity = extensive body surface area (>30 %) or immunocompromised host.

t.b: PaO2 <70 mm Hg or A‑a gradient >35 mm Hg → ICU admission, consider adjunctive steroids.
Opening pressure >250 mm H2O → therapeutic lumbar puncture every 24 h until <200 mm H2O.
Involvement of ≥2 non‑contiguous sites → treat as severe infection with amphotericin‑based regimen.
Urine antigen >0.5 ng/mL supports active disease; rising titers during therapy indicate treatment failure.

sections.p: Several bacterial, viral and non‑infectious diseases mimic fungal presentations; a focused comparison helps avoid misdiagnosis.
b: TB vs. endemic dimorphic pneumonia – both cause chronic cough and weight loss; TB shows caseating granulomas on sputum smear, whereas dimorphic fungi show antigen positivity.
Bacterial cellulitis vs. candidal intertrigo – cellulitis presents with warmth, swelling, systemic fever; candidal lesions have satellite papules and are often moist.
Viral esophagitis vs. Candida esophagitis – viral ulcers are shallow, multiple, and bleed on touch; Candida plaques are white, removable, and cause odynophagia.
Mucormycosis vs. aspergillosis – both cause sinus or pulmonary disease; Mucorales show broad aseptate hyphae with right‑angle branching on histology.

t.b: Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss; positive sputum AFB smear or GeneXpert distinguishes it from dimorphic fungi.
Erythema with well‑demarcated margins, fever, leukocytosis; lack of satellite papules and negative KOH point away from Candida.
Endoscopy shows shallow ulcers; PCR from biopsy differentiates from Candida plaques.
Rapid tissue necrosis, black eschar; histology shows broad, ribbon‑like aseptate hyphae with 90° branching, unlike septate Aspergillus.

sections.p: A systematic ladder guides clinicians from rapid stabilization to definitive antifungal therapy, with clear triggers for escalation or referral in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis with bedside microscopy (KOH, India ink, Giemsa) or rapid antigen test; if unavailable, base decision on clinical syndrome and risk factors.

2. Initiate empiric therapy targeting the most likely pathogen: fluconazole for mucocutaneous Candida or cryptococcal meningitis (if mild), amphotericin B deoxycholate (often with flucytosine) for severe disseminated disease, PCP‑directed TMP‑SMX, and itraconazole for sporotrichosis or dimorphic fungi.

3. Add adjunctive measures: control glucose, reduce steroids, start ART in HIV, ensure hydration and electrolyte balance, and manage intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningitis with therapeutic lumbar puncture.
4. Monitor clinical response daily (fever, respiratory status, lesion size) and laboratory markers (renal function, liver enzymes, complete blood count, serum β‑D‑glucan where available).

5. Escalate if no improvement within 72 h, if renal function worsens, or if organism is resistant: switch to lipid formulation amphotericin B, add flucytosine, or consider combination azole‑echinocandin therapy.
6. Refer to higher‑level centre for invasive disease requiring intensive care, neurosurgery, or unavailable susceptibility testing.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key toxicities of the main antifungal classes and practical steps to mitigate them, especially where monitoring capacity is limited.
b: Amphotericin B deoxycholate: nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, infusion‑related fever. Give pre‑hydration, monitor serum creatinine and potassium; replace potassium aggressively; consider lipid formulation if renal function declines.
Fluconazole: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, drug‑drug interactions via CYP2C9/2C19 inhibition. Check baseline liver enzymes; avoid concomitant drugs that prolong QT (e.g., quinine).

Itraconazole: hepatotoxicity, strong CYP3A4 inhibition, variable absorption with gastric acidity. Monitor liver enzymes; separate from antacids or proton‑pump inhibitors; use solution form if oral intake is poor.
TMP‑SMX (for PCP): bone‑marrow suppression, hyperkalemia, renal impairment. Check baseline CBC and electrolytes; hold if severe cytopenia or potassium >5.5 mmol/L; give folic acid supplementation.
Flucytosine: bone‑marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, renal clearance. Monitor CBC and renal function twice weekly; discontinue if neutropenia <1 × 10⁹/L or creatinine rises >50 %.

sections.p: Recognize disease‑specific complications and set objective thresholds for intensifying care or transferring the patient.
b: Cryptococcal meningitis: persistent headache, opening pressure >250 mm H₂O, or visual loss – perform therapeutic lumbar puncture every 24 h until pressure <200 mm H₂O; consider neurosurgical drainage if refractory.
Disseminated candidiasis: new organ involvement (e.g., endophthalmitis, osteomyelitis) or persistent fungemia after 72 h – add echinocandin or switch to lipid amphotericin B.

Dimorphic fungal pneumonia (Histoplasma, Blastomyces): progressive respiratory failure, hemoptysis, or radiographic cavitation – start amphotericin B deoxycholate; if renal risk, use lipid formulation.
Severe drug toxicity (e.g., rising creatinine >2 × baseline, neutropenia <0.5 × 10⁹/L) – stop offending agent, provide supportive care, and refer for specialist input.

sections.p: Host conditions and co‑medications that modify presentation, test interpretation, and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV: CD4 <200 cells/µL predisposes to PCP, cryptococcal meningitis, and disseminated histoplasmosis; CD4 count guides prophylaxis and urgency of antifungal therapy.
TB co‑infection: overlapping pulmonary infiltrates; sputum Xpert MTB/RIF may be negative in fungal disease; consider dual therapy and monitor for drug interactions (rifampicin reduces azole levels).
Malnutrition: blunted inflammatory signs, low albumin affecting drug binding; adjust dosing of highly protein‑bound agents and monitor for rapid clinical deterioration.
Pregnancy: avoid amphotericin B deoxycholate only if severe renal risk; fluconazole avoided in first trimester; use liposomal amphotericin B for life‑threatening disease.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia fuels Candida growth; tight glucose control improves outcomes; monitor for ketoacidosis when using high‑dose fluconazole.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort): induce CYP enzymes, reducing azole levels; ask specifically about traditional medicines.
Alcohol abuse: predisposes to liver dysfunction, increasing risk of azole hepatotoxicity; limit azole use if transaminases >3 × upper limit.
Renal failure: amphotericin B deoxycholate requires caution; use lipid formulation or dose‑adjusted flucytosine; monitor electrolytes closely.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for vulnerable populations and settings with limited laboratory capacity.
b: Children: prefer fluconazole for mucocutaneous disease; amphotericin B deoxycholate dosing based on body surface area; avoid itraconazole oral solution due to poor taste and absorption.
Pregnancy: liposomal amphotericin B is drug of choice for severe systemic infection; avoid azoles after first trimester; monitor fetal growth with ultrasound.
Elderly: higher risk of renal toxicity; start with lipid amphotericin B if possible; assess baseline cognition before using high‑dose steroids for PCP.
People with HIV: initiate ART after 2–4 weeks of antifungal induction to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; provide secondary prophylaxis until CD4 >200 cells/µL.

Low‑resource hospitals: rely on bedside KOH, Gram stain, and rapid antigen kits; use high‑dose fluconazole as bridge when amphotericin B unavailable; prioritize infection control and source reduction.

facts: Fungal cell wall contains chitin and β‑D‑glucan, key for immune detection.
Thermal dimorphism: mold at ≤25 °C, yeast at 37 °C.
CD4 < 200 cells/µL markedly increases risk of PCP and cryptococcal meningitis.
Serum (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan > 80 pg/mL supports diagnosis of PCP, candidemia, and invasive aspergillosis.
India ink positive capsule indicates Cryptococcus neoformans; opening pressure > 250 mmH₂O requires therapeutic lumbar puncture.
Fluconazole is first‑line for uncomplicated oropharyngeal candidiasis and for consolidation therapy of cryptococcal meningitis.
Liposomal amphotericin B is the renal‑sparing alternative when amphotericin B deoxycholate is contraindicated.

vivas.q: Define opportunistic systemic fungal infection and give two common examples in HIV patients.
vivas.a: Infections that occur when immunity is compromised; examples: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cryptococcal meningitis.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps differentiate PCP from bacterial pneumonia?
vivas.a: Serum (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan; markedly elevated in PCP, usually normal in bacterial pneumonia.

vivas.q: Why is amphotericin B deoxycholate used with extreme caution in renal failure?
vivas.a: It is nephrotoxic, causing tubular injury and electrolyte wasting; monitor renal function and consider lipid formulation.

vivas.q: Distinguish Histoplasma capsulatum infection from tuberculosis on chest X‑ray.
vivas.a: Histoplasma often shows diffuse reticulonodular pattern with mediastinal calcified nodes; TB shows cavitary upper‑lobe lesions and hilar adenopathy.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line treatment for uncomplicated oropharyngeal candidiasis?
vivas.a: Fluconazole oral loading dose followed by daily dosing for 7–14 days.

vivas.q: Explain why azoles are not used for induction therapy of severe cryptococcal meningitis.
vivas.a: Azoles have slower fungicidal activity; amphotericin B plus flucytosine achieves rapid CSF sterilisation, improving survival.

vivas.q: A farmer presents with a chronic hand lesion containing yellow granules; which fungus is most likely?
Identify the fungal class with broad, ribbon‑like aseptate hyphae and wide‑angle branching.
Which genus produces aflatoxin B1 linked to hepatic carcinoma?
vivas.a: Aspergillus (especially A. flavus and A. parasiticus).

vivas.q: At what temperatures do dimorphic fungi display mold versus yeast forms?
State a fundamental metabolic difference between true fungi and plants.
vivas.a: Fungi are heterotrophic, lacking chlorophyll and photosynthesis; they obtain carbon by absorption.

vivas.q: Fungi lacking a known sexual stage are placed in which taxonomic group?
vivas.a: They are classified within existing phyla (e.g., Ascomycota, Basidiomycota) based on asexual characteristics.

vivas.q: Which plasma‑membrane component is the target of polyene and azole antifungals?
vivas.a: Ergosterol biosynthesis pathway; polyenes bind ergosterol, azoles inhibit lanosterol 14‑α‑demethylase.

vivas.q: Which fungal phylum accounts for ~85 % of human pathogenic species?
In a resource‑limited setting without culture, how would you diagnose PCP?
vivas.a: Combine clinical picture (dry cough, hypoxia, CD4 < 200) with elevated serum (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan and, if possible, induced sputum or BAL showing cysts on Giemsa stain.

vivas.q: Why is liposomal amphotericin B preferred over deoxycholate formulation in renal impairment?
vivas.a: Liposomal formulation has reduced nephrotoxicity while retaining fungicidal activity.

vivas.q: What key history points raise suspicion for endemic dimorphic infection?
vivas.a: Travel or residence in endemic areas, exposure to soil or bird/bat droppings, and chronic respiratory symptoms.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old man with HIV (CD4 120) presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough and normal chest X‑ray. Which test is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Bronchoalveolar lavage visualises Pneumocystis cysts; serum β‑D‑glucan is supportive but not definitive.

mcqs.q: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis has an opening pressure of 300 mmH₂O. What is the next immediate step?
o: Perform therapeutic lumbar puncture to drain CSF
mcqs.e: Therapeutic lumbar puncture reduces intracranial pressure and improves outcomes.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old farmer has a subcutaneous nodule with black granules. Microscopy shows thin, branching hyphae. Which organism is most likely?
mcqs.e: Yellow/black granules with branching hyphae describe eumycetoma caused by Madurella.

mcqs.q: Which fungal class is characterized by broad, ribbon‑like aseptate hyphae with right‑angle branching?
mcqs.e: Mucorales (formerly Zygomycetes) have aseptate, wide‑angle branching hyphae.

mcqs.q: A child presents with oral thrush that can be scraped off, no systemic signs. Which drug is first‑line?
mcqs.e: Fluconazole is the standard first‑line for uncomplicated oropharyngeal candidiasis.

cases.v: 28‑year‑old woman, HIV positive, CD4 90, presents with headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness. Opening pressure 280 mmH₂O; CSF India ink shows encapsulated yeast; CSF CrAg positive.

qs.q: What is the immediate management step?
qs.a: Perform therapeutic lumbar puncture to lower opening pressure below 200 mmH₂O, repeat as needed.

qs.q: What induction therapy should be started?
qs.a: Amphotericin B deoxycholate plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks.
High‑dose fluconazole consolidation for 8 weeks, then low‑dose maintenance until immune reconstitution.

cases.v: 12‑year‑old boy from a rural area presents with a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer on the forearm after a thorn injury. The ulcer contains yellow granules; microscopy shows thin, septate hyphae.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Eumycetoma, most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis.

qs.q: What is the cornerstone of treatment?
qs.a: Surgical excision of the granules combined with prolonged itraconazole therapy.

qs.q: Which bedside sign helps differentiate mycetoma from sporotrichosis?
qs.a: Presence of visible granules (grains) within the sinus tract; sporotrichosis lacks grains.

mistakes: Prescribing fluconazole alone for induction of severe cryptococcal meningitis.
Using amphotericin B deoxycholate in a patient with CrCl < 30 mL/min without renal monitoring or lipid formulation.
Confusing Sporothrix schenckii as the cause of mycetoma with yellow granules.
Assuming a normal chest X‑ray rules out PCP; early PCP may have a normal film.
Neglecting therapeutic lumbar puncture in cryptococcal meningitis with high opening pressure.
Treating all dimorphic infections with azoles only; severe disease requires amphotericin B‑based regimens.
Omitting flucytosine from the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis when available.
Relying on culture alone in low‑resource settings; bedside microscopy and antigen tests are essential.
